rv.q: The musical adaptation of F. Scott Fitzgerald's classic novel brings lavish spectacle to Broadway, though it sometimes struggles to capture the source material's deeper themes.
This revisionary attempt to turn “The Great Gatsby” into a clown car of passionate entanglements skids off the road when calamity is meant to strike.
For any fan of “The Great Gatsby,” though, it's likely you'll have moments of wanting more, of missing out on all the subtext, grit, and suffering beneath the sequins.
It’s a perfectly winsome scene, and a highlight of this ultimately underwhelming new adaptation
To audiences hungry for glitz this year, The Good Gatsby may be good enough.
This new musical makes you feel very little, except for when Howland's lush melodies reach their climaxes.
Somewhere, Scott must be cackling.
Missteps in story and direction would be more or less fine if the show itself was entertaining. But it's only tepidly so.
This is modern day American musical theatre at its finest, that feels right for the whole family.
If The Great Gatsby doesn’t have the makings of a long-term Broadway resident, it’s become, in its newly minted tension and decadence, a welcome visitor.
The Great Gatsby is a great big Broadway extravaganza that may dazzle viewers at first but, much like the green light, perfection remains close, yet just out of reach.
Ultimately, this might not be a Great Gatsby that English teachers will agree with, but if you’re going to drop $200 on a Broadway ticket, it certainly gives you your money’s worth.
Though it's too glossy an adaptation of the classic novel, The Great Gatsby presents rich performances and design.
It's a mesmerizing yet disconcerting, distorted dance as the party roars on ("and on and on and on")...
If all you’re seeking is a spectacle, you will get one.

But, with one exception, this last Broadway musical to open this season is also just not very satisfying to me as a musical, despite (or in part because of) the many ways it strains, loudly, to proclaim itself a quintessential Broadway musical.
In other words, the transfiguration of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby is, sorry to report, a travesty.
It’s debatable whether one of American literature’s most mysterious characters should ever sing. What Gatsby should definitely not ever do is lead a chorus of tap dancers.

On the contrary, I felt I had seen a musical with all the winning elements of a great Broadway show—visually beautiful, thoroughly engaging, magically fun, emotionally gripping, and enjoyable in every way.
Seeing a musical like The Great Gatsby come alive on stage in such a beautifully realized production is not only surprising but invigorating.
Overall, “The Great Gatsby” was a lavish and entertaining new Broadway musical.

But theatergoers who hunger to see a live musical staging of Fitzgerald's 1925 masterpiece with an eye-popping set, exquisite period costumes, and a first-rate cast who can sing, this is your golden opportunity.
While this approach is certainly not as elevated as one of Fitzgerald’s complex metaphors, it sure is a lot of campy fun.
This is a surprisingly enjoyable telling of the familiar story.
The Great Gatsby musical is ushered forward in a pretty straightforward approach but never really finds its continuity or resonance.
…a real puzzler, a show that can't make up its mind about what it wants to be.
Simply put, if you treasure the novel, don't come to the theatre.
Nobody who’s read and admired the Fitzgerald novel wants to see a tap-dancing Gatsby.
But, at intermission, director Marc Bruni's production had me wondering, why is this even being done?
Overall, there’s a lot of flash and little substance to generate any sympathy.
